subject: Geography
chapter: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
central_question: How do pollution, urban waste, migration, slums and land degradation arise from uneven human-environment relations, and what community and policy responses can reduce their impacts?
in_scope_units: Environmental pollution and classification by medium
Water pollution: sources, river examples, health effects and Namami Gange
Air pollution, urban smog, acid rain and health effects
Noise pollution, sources, measurement and spatial decline
Urban waste disposal, health hazards and the Daurala restoration case
Rural–urban migration and the Ramesh case study
Problems of slums and the Dharavi description
Land degradation, wastelands and natural and human causes
Jhabua watershed-management case study and community participation
banned_topics: Detailed national water-resource availability and irrigation demand, which belong to Water Resources
Detailed urban-settlement classification, which belongs to Settlement Geography

known_pitfalls.claim: Pollution and pollutant mean the same thing.
known_pitfalls.correction: Pollution is the degraded environmental condition or process, while pollutants are the substances or forms of energy causing it.

known_pitfalls.claim: Natural sources are the main concern in India’s water pollution.
known_pitfalls.correction: The chapter states that human industrial, agricultural and cultural activities are the real causes of concern, with industry the most significant contributor.
The chapter argues that waste can be treated as a resource for energy and compost, and ragpickers recover items with value.

known_pitfalls.claim: Every degraded land parcel is already wasteland.
known_pitfalls.correction: All degraded land is not necessarily wasteland, but unchecked degradation may convert land into wasteland.

known_pitfalls.claim: Rural–urban migration has only economic benefits.
known_pitfalls.correction: Remittances may improve family welfare, but migrants may face low wages, temporary work, cultural adjustment and family separation.

recommended_example_progression: Use NCERT Exercise 2(i) to distinguish pollution from pollutants.
Use NCERT Exercise 3(i) to describe water pollution in India.
Use NCERT Exercise 2(iii) to organise urban-waste problems.
Use NCERT Exercise 1(iv) to connect push and pull factors with migration.
Use NCERT Exercise 3(iii) to propose measures for reducing land degradation.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The chapter ends with EXERCISES 1–3: four MCQs, four short-answer questions and three long-answer questions.
